title: Explainable AI and well‐to‐wheel lifecycle fusion for predictive sustainability assessment of bioethanol–gasoline blends
content:
Abstract

Ethanol-gasoline blends are a promising strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving energy security. Studies have largely considered engine performance and lifecycle emissions separately, with little exploration of the connection between tank-to-wheel and well-to-wheel analysis. Performance, emissions and sustainability characteristics of a single-cylinder spark-ignition engine fuelled with six ethanol–petrol blends were experimental investigations at five engine loads. A Gaussian Process Regression model was developed and validated with leave-one-out and leave-one-blend-out cross-validation to interpolate the intermediate blends E22 and E27, and it achieved strong accuracy across all directly measured responses (R 2 = 0.9976–0.9998). The model was interpreted through SHAP analysis, revealing engine load as the main factor controlling performance and sustainability metrics, and ethanol content having a higher influence on the composition of exhaust emission. Multi-objective Pareto optimisation, verified with independent objective pairings to ensure robustness, revealed E20 as the optimal solution for engine-side objectives at full load, shifting to E30 at 80% load when lifecycle carbon intensity was incorporated. The fusion of experimental tank-to-wheel data with reconciled literature-based well-to-tank emissions, covering the well-to-wheel life cycle, also showed that the life cycle carbon advantage of second-generation (2G) over first-generation (1G) ethanol sourcing. The 2G lifecycle carbon advantage over 1G ethanol holds under mature processing but not India's current pilot-scale technology, and depends strongly on emission-factor ranges. This explainable, data-driven framework evaluates ethanol blends for engine performance, emissions and sustainability, supporting biofuel policy.
